explanation:
## The two searches

```rust
fn find_name<'a>(names: &'a [String], prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a String> {
    for n in names {
        if n.starts_with(prefix) {
            return Some(n);
        }
    }
    None
}
```

The bare `None` at the end is the function's value when the loop completes - no
flag, no sentinel. And `Some(n)` wraps a **borrow** of the element, so nothing is
copied and the caller gets a view into the list.

## What `Option` buys over `-1`

The C++ version of `position_of` returned `-1`, and that worked because an index
cannot be negative. Three things change here:

**The type is different.** `Option<usize>` is not a `usize`. Try to use it as
one and the program does not compile, so "I forgot to check" is not a failure
mode that exists.

**No value is stolen.** `Option<i64>` represents every `i64` plus nothing, so
the trick survives being applied to a function that returns a *value* from the
data rather than an index - which is exactly where the `-1` convention breaks.

**The check is not optional.** A `match` must cover every variant:

```rust
match find_name(&names, query) {
    Some(found) => ...,
    // forgetting None here:
}
```

```
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `None` not covered
```

That is the difference from `std::optional` in C++, which has all of the first
two properties and none of the third - `*opt` on an empty optional is undefined
behaviour, and nothing makes you call `has_value()` first.

And `Option` costs nothing. `Option<&T>` is a single pointer, with `None`
represented as the null pointer, because the compiler knows a reference is never
null. So the safe version compiles to the same code as the C pointer-returning
version, with the check enforced.

## Three ways in, and when each is right

**`match`** - both outcomes do real work:

```rust
match find_name(&names, query) {
    Some(found) => writeln!(out, "prefix {} {}", query, found),
    None => writeln!(out, "prefix {} none", query),
}
```

Exhaustive, so the compiler is checking you handled everything. This is the
default; reach for the others when `match` is heavier than the situation.

**`if let`** - one arm is interesting and the other is a fallback. It is
`match` with one pattern and an optional `else`, and it reads as a conditional
rather than as a dispatch.

**`map` and `unwrap_or`** - you want to transform the value if it is there and
substitute a default if not, with no branch written at all:

```rust
let len = find_name(&names, query).map(|s| s.len()).unwrap_or(0);
```

`map` applies the closure inside a `Some` and passes `None` through untouched.
This chaining style is where Rust's error handling stops feeling like checking
and starts feeling like a pipeline. The ones worth learning early:

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `map(f)` | `Some(x)` to `Some(f(x))`, `None` stays `None` |
| `and_then(f)` | like `map` but `f` itself returns an `Option` - flattens |
| `unwrap_or(d)` | the value, or `d` |
| `unwrap_or_else(f)` | the value, or `f()` - when the default is expensive |
| `ok_or(e)` | turn an `Option` into a `Result`, supplying the error |
| `filter(p)` | `Some(x)` only if `p(x)`, else `None` |

`unwrap()` is also there and panics on `None`. It is right in a test, in a
prototype, and where you can prove the value exists - and in production code
each one is a potential crash, which is why `expect("why this cannot fail")` is
preferred: it makes the claim visible and puts it in the panic message.

## The lifetime, and why one function needs it

```rust
fn find_name<'a>(names: &'a [String], prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a String>
```

The returned reference points into `names`, so it must not outlive it. With one
reference parameter the compiler assumes the output borrows from it and you write
nothing - that is lifetime elision. With **two** reference parameters it cannot
guess which one the return value came from, so it asks:

```
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the
          signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `names` or `prefix`
```

`'a` answers exactly that question, and it names a constraint rather than a
duration: *the returned reference is valid for as long as `names` is.* Having
said it, the compiler will reject a caller that drops the list and keeps the
result.

`position_of` needs none of this, because `usize` is a plain value that borrows
nothing. That contrast is the whole of what lifetimes are for: they appear only
where a reference escapes a function, and they describe a relationship between
borrows that already exist.

## `starts_with("")` is true

Every string starts with the empty string, so an empty query matches the first
name in the list - which is why one hidden case exists and why the statement
spells it out. The vacuous answer is the mathematically right one, the same way
an empty sum is 0 and an empty string is a palindrome.

The `_` placeholder is a format workaround: input is whitespace-separated, so an
empty token cannot be written. Worth noticing as a general point about
stdin-based protocols - "no value" needs an encoding, and picking one that cannot
collide with real data is part of designing the format. A length-prefixed or
quoted format would not need the hack.

## Comparing a `&String` with a `&str`

```rust
if n == wanted        // n: &String, wanted: &str
```

This works because `String` implements `PartialEq<str>`, so the comparison
compares contents rather than requiring the types to match. It is one of a small
number of cross-type impls the standard library provides specifically because
`String`/`&str` is such a common pair.

Which is also why `starts_with` takes `&str` and the function signature does
too. Taking `&String` there would have forced callers to allocate - and the
whole point of `&str` is that it works on a literal, a slice, or a borrowed
`String`, with no copy in any of the three cases.
